ext.research_question: Does team-level, in-game momentum exist in NBA basketball, and can a pause in play interrupt it? The test is whether a TV timeout (mandatory, scheduled independently of the game) during a scoring run reduces the momentumed team's subsequent scoring, compared with matched runs that are not interrupted (abstract p.117; Sec. 1 p.118-119).
ext.theory: Momentum is defined as team-level serial correlation in scoring: after unanswered points, a team scores more than its baseline would predict (Sec. 1 p.118; Sec. 2 p.119). The paper contrasts this with the hot-hand literature (Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky 1985, and later critiques by Miller and Sanjuro 2018a, Bocskocsky et al. 2014, Csapo et al. 2015). Coaches call timeouts when they expect them to stop a run, so coach-called timeouts are endogenous and naive before/after comparisons are biased (Sec. 2 p.120; Sec. 3 p.121). If timeouts stop momentum, then exogenous pauses should not affect scoring only if timeouts are ineffective, which gives a testable prediction (Sec. 3 p.120). The paper also cites Den Hartigh and Gernigon (2018) that pauses let players recover from negative momentum even without coaching.
ext.data: Play-by-play scoring-play rows from BigDataBall (2020) for 13 NBA seasons, 2004-05 to 2016-17, including playoffs (Sec. 4 p.122). Each row is one scoring play and records lineups, points, time remaining, a following-timeout flag, and whether that timeout was a TV timeout. Unit of analysis: a scoring run (treated = run interrupted by a TV timeout; control = run with no timeout), matched 1:1 to its nearest untreated neighbour on propensity scores from logistic regression (MatchIt; unmatched observations discarded; matched pairs can come from different games and teams) (Sec. 4 p.122-123). Sample sizes in Table 3 (p.125): 5,148 matched runs (run >= 6), 576 (run >= 10), 48 (run >= 15). Table 4 (no substitutions by either team): 4,644. Monte Carlo (Table 5): 130,000 simulated scoring plays, regression n = 1,336. Full-season N and number of games are not stated in the extracted text. Fig. 1 notes 11.85% of runs reach six or more unanswered points (p.123).
ext.method: Matched observational design with a natural experiment. Propensity-score matching (logistic regression, nearest neighbour; Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983; Ho et al. 2011, MatchIt), with Mahalanobis matching as a robustness check (Table A2, not in text). Outcome: points scored by the momentumed team in the three minutes of game time after the TV timeout (or the run's next play). Estimator: Poisson regression (count outcome, Sec. 4 p.124; Table 3 p.125), with covariates run size and substitutions by each team. Robustness: negative binomial (Appendix B, reported as substantively identical), alternative windows from 60 to 240 seconds (Appendix D), coaches' timeouts as treatment (Appendix E), and a Monte Carlo placebo with zero true effect (Table 5, Fig. 6, p.127-128). Model comparison by bootstrapped AIC, 1,000 resamples of size 48 or 576 (Fig. 3, p.124-126).
ext.scope: Population: NBA regular-season and playoff games, 2004-05 to 2016-17 (13 seasons), team-level momentum within a game. Institutional setting: NBA rulebook TV-timeout procedure (first stoppage after the 9:00 mark of the second quarter unless a timeout was already called in that quarter; 100-second TV timeouts; coaches' timeouts 60 or 100 seconds) (Sec. 1 p.118). Era: pre-2017 NBA. The paper argues the question matters for all sports (Sec. 6 p.131) but tests basketball only. No seasons after 2016-17 and no notational or player-tracking data were used.
ext.identification:
Treatment is a TV timeout occurring during a run. The paper treats its timing as random assignment: TV timeouts are mandatory, fixed by rulebook procedure, and cannot be self-selected by teams (Sec. 3 p.121). Key assumption, stated by the authors as the key to the paper: TV timeouts are exogenous to momentum and to strategy (Sec. 3 p.120; Sec. 5.3 p.129). Propensity-score matching balances observables (Table A1, no significant imbalance, not in text). Substitutions by each team are a proxy for strategic change during the stoppage, and matching on them isolates the stoppage effect (Sec. 3 p.122). Substitutions can happen at dead balls, not only timeouts, which the matching design relies on. Identification also relies on the Monte Carlo placebo (null result, Table 5) and on subset tests (no substitutions; garbage time excluded; crunch time excluded; first TV timeouts only).</identification>
<parameter name="measures">["Momentum indicator m = 1 if the team scored at least 6 unanswered points immediately before the TV timeout (Eq. 1, p.122); alternative thresholds 10 and 15", "Run size: unanswered points by the momentumed team", "Substitutions by momentumed team and by opposing team (0 to 5 players), counted during the TV timeout for treated runs and at the dead ball after the basket for controls (p.123-124)", "Dependent variable: points scored by the momentumed team in the next 3 minutes of game time (alternative windows 60 s to 4 min)", "Model fit: AIC and log-likelihood, bootstrapped for comparability across sample sizes"]
ext.theory_notes: Momentum is a team-level, within-game effect (scoring unanswered points), not the individual hot hand.

key_findings.finding: A TV timeout during a run lowers the momentumed team's points in the next 3 minutes. Coefficient -0.119 (SE 0.012), p < 0.01, so e^b - 1 = -11.2%. Average gap about 0.56 points.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.117; Sec. 5.1 p.124; Table 3 col. 1 p.125; Conclusion p.130

key_findings.finding: Opposing-team substitutions also reduce the momentumed team's scoring, by less than the TV timeout does (about half as strong, per text).
key_findings.numbers: b = -0.077 (0.017), e^b - 1 = -7.4%; text says TV effect is about 50% larger

key_findings.finding: Substitutions by the momentumed team have the largest effect in the 6-point model. The authors read this as breaking up the momentumed lineup.
The TV timeout effect grows for longer runs. Opposing-team substitutions lose significance at longer runs.
No mean reversion: the current-run-size coefficient is not significant in any model.
key_findings.numbers: Text: .001. Table 3 shows -0.002 (0.003), -0.003 (0.009), -0.018 (0.031). The two disagree; see limitations.

key_findings.finding: The effect is largest right after play resumes. It is about four times as large in the first minute as in the 3-minute window. The 0.56-point figure is therefore a lower bound.
Model fit favours the 6- and 10-point run definitions over 15-point runs. The 6-point model fits as well as the 10-point model.
Effect is consistent across run sizes up to 17 points, so it is not an artefact of a particular threshold.
key_findings.numbers: TV timeouts reduce scoring for runs of 17 points or fewer

key_findings.finding: TV timeouts with no substitutions by either team still reduce scoring, by about 41% less than timeouts with substitutions. The authors attribute about 59% of the total effect to stoppage of play and the rest to strategy change.
key_findings.numbers: b = -0.068 (0.013), -6.57%, n = 4,644; about 41% smaller than Table 3 effect

key_findings.finding: Substitution counts do not rise with run length, which argues against substitutions being a strategic response to runs.
key_findings.numbers: slope not distinguishable from zero (regression not shown in text)

key_findings.finding: Monte Carlo placebo with zero true momentum (130,000 plays, one TV timeout per 50 plays): the TV timeout coefficient is null.
The TV timeout coefficient shrinks as the outcome window lengthens. There is no significant effect in the 3-to-4-minute window.
key_findings.numbers: effect weakens with longer window; no significant effect between minutes 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Robustness: garbage-time exclusion, crunch-time exclusion, first TV timeouts only, and negative binomial all leave results substantively unchanged. Coaches' timeouts give a slightly larger effect, and the difference from TV timeouts is not significant.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.2 p.128-129; Appendices B, C, E (not in text)
key_findings.numbers: no numbers given in main text for these subsets

limitations: Authors: TV timeouts may not be exogenous to gameplay change. Strategy changes other than substitutions (defensive or pick-and-roll assignments, speeches) are not measured (Sec. 5.3 p.129).
Authors: no readily available notational or tracking data, so non-substitution strategy changes are not tested directly (p.129).
Authors: estimates for runs of 15 or more points rest on n = 48; the 30.79% estimate should be read cautiously (p.125).
Authors: matching on more covariates would shrink the already small samples (5,148 / 576 / 48) (p.129).
Authors concede strategic changes probably do occur during TV timeouts; the checks suggest they do not explain the results but do not rule them out (p.129-130).
Authors: the TV timeout effect and the coaches'-timeout effect are both present, so TV timeouts contain elements of stoppage and strategy (p.129).

Reader observation, not stated by the authors: the text reports the mean-reversion coefficient as .001, but Table 3 reports -0.002, -0.003 and -0.018 for the three run thresholds. The text and table disagree.

Reader observation: the text says even one unused timeout adds points to the opponent's score (p.130), but no supporting numbers appear in the main text; the claim may depend on the unseen appendices.

Reader observation: the paper recommends that coaches of momentumed teams avoid substitutions during TV timeouts (p.130). That conclusion treats the substitution count, a strategy proxy the authors did not randomise, as a causal lever.

Reader observation: the 6-unanswered-point threshold was chosen a priori; only 11.85% of runs meet it (Fig. 1 p.123). Sensitivity to threshold is shown only at 10 and 15, and the 15-point models have n = 48.
Reader observation: the appendices (A-E) were not in the extracted text, so balance tests, Mahalanobis and negative binomial results are reported only as the main text describes them.

rel.summary_md:
Weimer, Steinert-Threlkeld and Coltin test whether team-level scoring momentum exists in the NBA. Their identification idea is the transferable part. Coach-called timeouts are a response to momentum, so comparing scoring before and after them is biased. TV timeouts fall at points the rulebook fixes, so they act as near-random pauses. The authors take scoring runs of 6 or more unanswered points from 13 seasons (2004-05 to 2016-17) and match runs interrupted by a TV timeout 1:1 on propensity scores to runs with no timeout. In 5,148 matched runs, a TV timeout cuts the running team's points in the next 3 minutes by 11.2% (b = -0.119, about 0.56 points). The effect is larger for longer runs (n = 576 and 48), about 41% smaller when neither team substitutes (n = 4,644), and fades after 3 minutes. A Monte Carlo placebo with zero true momentum returns a null coefficient (b = 0.002, n = 1,336), so the result is not produced by how runs were selected.

None of the basketball findings transfer to Melange, Mentat or Terrier. The method lessons do. First, a treatment someone chooses (a lobbyist's contact, a PAC's spend) is endogenous in the same way a coach's timeout is, so naive before/after or contact-conditioned correlations are biased. Second, a simulated null is a cheap way to show that an estimator or a selection rule does not manufacture effects. The system's prospective receptivity contract already limits its claims to forecasting. The contact-conditioned arm it plans is exactly the coach-timeout design this paper warns against. The engine has no negative control: a repo search of fec/engine for placebo, negative control and null simulation found none.

bearings.paper_claim: Comparing outcomes before and after a coach-called timeout is fallacious because coaches call timeouts to stop momentum. Only an exogenously timed pause (TV timeout), matched 1:1 on propensity scores, identifies the effect: -11.2% points over 3 minutes, n = 5,148 matched runs.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1 p.118; Sec. 3 p.120-121 (Table 1, ideal experiment); Sec. 4 p.122-123; Table 3 p.125
bearings.system_side: H2 scores pressure_mult against |overall-tier movement| with an unadjusted cross-sectional Spearman. The protocol text plans an engaged-only arm restricted to members the In-contact log marks as engaged. That arm is NOT_IMPLEMENTED, and CLAIM_SCOPE limits the contract to forecasting, not spending effects.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/outcome_contract.py:17-21 (protocol, engaged-only H2); fec/engine/outcome_contract.py:277-283 (unadjusted Spearman; engaged_only NOT_IMPLEMENTED); fec/members/receptivity_sensitivity.py:14-16
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transfer is about design logic, not effect size. Lobbying contact is chosen by the lobbyist, often for members expected to move, just as coaches pick timeouts. An engaged-only H2 would therefore confound pressure_mult with targeting. Unless contact timing is exogenous (for example a scheduled fly-in or a randomized outreach order) or matched on targeting covariates (tier, PERS, party), an engaged-only rho cannot be read as receptivity. The unconditional H1 and H2, as forecasts, are not affected. NBA play is a closed system with exact timing; congressional contact data has neither property. Weimer's estimates are themselves single-study and observational with matching.

bearings.paper_claim: A Monte Carlo placebo with zero true momentum (130,000 simulated plays, one TV timeout per 50 plays) yields a null treatment coefficient (b = 0.002, SE 0.022, n = 1,336). The authors use it as a negative control showing the effect is not an artifact of how runs were selected.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.2 p.127-128; Table 5; Fig. 6; Conclusion p.130
bearings.system_side: The discipline already uses a simulated null to calibrate its protocol: a joint-null false-pass simulation (pass-both-panels about 1.5-2%) limited each Big Five trait to one more look.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the general practice of simulating under a known null to check that a selection or gating rule cannot manufacture a pass. It says nothing about the 1.5-2% figure or about pre-registration itself. That simulation is applied to protocol false-pass rates, not to the engine's outcome estimators.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper's Monte Carlo is a negative control for an estimator applied to observed data: simulate the data with no effect, re-run the estimator, and expect a null.
bearings.system_side: The scenario runner uses Monte Carlo as a forward model. It compares baseline and scenario spread under common random numbers (MC 40, SEED 7), so a null scenario gives a zero delta by construction. That is a code identity check, not a negative control on any inferred effect.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/scenario.py:38-53 (CRN cascade); fec/engine/scenario.py:102-106 (baseline vs scenario spread and flip deltas)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul highlighted Weimer's Monte Carlo, but the two uses of Monte Carlo are different. The scenario runner's deltas are model outputs, not estimates, so a Weimer-style placebo applies only to empirical estimators that read observed outcomes, such as the forecasters and the contract. It does not validate the cascade.

bearings.paper_claim: The point estimate shrinks steadily as the outcome window lengthens (60 to 240 s), and there is no significant effect between minutes 3 and 4. The headline estimate depends on the chosen window, and the first-minute effect is about 4 times the 3-minute effect.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.1 p.124; Sec. 5.2 p.129; Appendix D (not in extracted text)
bearings.system_side: The sensitivity harness sweeps receptivity constants and MC budgets and seeds (top-20 overlap >= 18 = ROBUST). The contract fixes one outcome window (at least 60 days) and sweeps no windows.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/mc_stability_check.py:13-17 (MC/SEED sweep only); fec/engine/outcome_contract.py:258-259 (single window, days < 60 => UNDERPOWERED)
bearings.transfer_conditions: This suggests pre-registering a small set of outcome windows inside the contract lock, not choosing one afterward, which would be basis-shopping. The paper's minute-scale decay says nothing about congressional time scales.

gaps_exposed: No negative control or placebo exists for any empirical estimator in fec/engine. A repo search of fec/engine for placebo, negative control and null simulation found none. A simulated-null run of the cosponsor forecaster or the H1/H2 scorer (shuffled predictors, or a synthetic panel with zero effect) would show whether selection or roster filtering can produce a rho of +.20 by itself.

The planned engaged-only H2 arm (outcome_contract.py:17-21) conditions on lobbyist-chosen contact, which is endogenous like a coach's timeout. No exogenous source of contact timing and no matching design is specified. The arm is NOT_IMPLEMENTED (line 283), so this can be fixed before any contact contract is written.

The contract's H1/H2 Spearman is unadjusted: no party or chamber strata and no matched comparison. Any later attempt to read it as more than a forecast would need the matching or exogenous-assignment structure the paper models.
The outcome window is a single choice (at least 60 days) with no pre-registered window sweep. The paper shows estimates can change substantially with window length.
flags: Category conflict: one of Paul's bibliography files puts this paper in the folder 'Adjacent', but the component positions place it in the Causal & Methodological folder. I categorized it Causal & Methodological because only its method transfers. Paul may want to settle which folder it belongs in.

Paul's highlight of the closing recommendation (coaches of momentumed teams should not substitute during TV timeouts) rests on substitution counts that were not randomized. It is a causal claim on a non-randomized proxy and should not be used as a model for prescriptive rules in Melange.
Text-table inconsistency in the source: the text gives the mean-reversion coefficient as .001, while Table 3 shows -0.002, -0.003 and -0.018. Quote Table 3 if this paper is cited at all.
No conflict with D-021, D-025, D-104..D-108, the two rejected SNA proposals, or the barred influence language. The paper makes no network, LDA or reciprocity claim.
This analysis is UNVERIFIED under DE-062 until a second path reproduces the bearings, in particular the finding that the engine has no negative control.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's bibliography entries for this paper contain only the citation, with no takeaways. His 57 highlights mark the identification argument (endogenous coach timeouts versus exogenous TV timeouts), propensity matching, and the Monte Carlo negative control. The component positions tie it to competitive-cascade-crn, scenario-runner and single-look-discipline as a Monte Carlo tool or negative control. That reading is partly off target. The engine's Monte Carlo (CRN cascades in scenario.py and budget_frontier.py) is a forward simulator, and a null scenario returns zero by construction, so Weimer's placebo does not validate it. What the paper validates is putting a simulated null on empirical estimators, and the system does this only for look false-pass rates (brain note line 56). The sharper lesson in his highlights, that a self-selected intervention biases before/after comparisons, bears most on the engaged-only H2 arm of the prospective contract. His notes do not mention that arm. I found no bearing on competitive-cascade-crn.

related.why: Both papers caution about causal identification in observational panels. Imai & Kim cover two-way fixed effects, Weimer covers matching on a natural experiment, and both bear on reading Melange's and Mentat's observational looks.

Both papers deal with confounding when the treatment is chosen strategically (ad buys, coach timeouts). Blackwell's correction for unmeasured confounding answers the limitation Weimer concedes: unmeasured strategy changes during timeouts.
Kalla & Broockman randomize the treatment, which is the ideal experiment of Weimer's Table 1. It is the political-domain template for exogenous contact that the engaged-only H2 arm would need.
Both papers use Monte Carlo simulation. Harrison gives general practice, and Weimer applies it as a negative control, a different use from the engine's forward cascades.
